Alien Worlds: Sanctuaries or Wastelands? The latest piece from award-winning sci-fi author and science communicator Omara Williams as she looks to space in the search for habitable alien planets. 12 August 2026 More than 6,200 planets have now been confirmed beyond our solar system. Award-winning sci-fi author and science communicator Omara Williams explores how astronomers find them, which nearby worlds look most promising, and what it would really take for an alien planet to be habitable. Artist impression showing the surface of the planet Proxima b orbiting the red dwarf star Proxima Centauri, the closest star to the Solar System. Credit: ESO/M. Kornmesser. For centuries, people looked up at the night sky and wondered whether other stars had planets similar to our own. Now we know that the answer is a definite yes . Astronomers have confirmed more than 6,200 exoplanets orbiting stars beyond our solar system, and billions more are likely to exist in the Milky Way alone. The quest to find other worlds like our own has been one of the most exciting scientific endeavours of the last few decades. The discovery of the first exoplanets—planets orbiting stars other than our Sun—opened the door to a Universe of possibilities. The first confirmed exoplanets were announced in 1992 by a team led by Polish astronomer Aleksander Wolszczan; they were not found orbiting a star like our Sun but instead circled a pulsar (a rapidly rotating remnant of a star that has exploded) called PSR B1257+12. Their presence was determined by detecting small irregularities in the pulsar’s regular radio pulses, caused by the planets’ gravitational influence. However, the discovery that truly captured the world’s imagination was the detection of 51 Pegasi b in 1995, 50 light-years away. This breakthrough was so impactful because it revealed a planet orbiting a star very much like our Sun, showing that planets could exist around stars similar to our own. It marked a turning point in the search for other worlds and opened the door to the thousands of exoplanet discoveries that followed. The Hunt for Distant Worlds Finding a planet many light-years away is an immense challenge. Planets are tiny and dim compared to their host stars, so astronomers use clever methods to detect their presence, often by observing the effect they have on their star. The Transit Method: This approach has accounted for the vast majority of exoplanet discoveries and consists of observing the slight decrease in a star’s brightness when a planet passes in front of it—that is, when a transit occurs. It is a technique of remarkable accuracy, similar to spotting the drop in light from a huge searchlight when an ant crawls across it from a great distance. Missions such as Kepler and TESS have employed this method to find thousands of planets. The Radial Velocity, or “Wobble,” Method: This technique was used to discover 51 Pegasi b, the first exoplanet confirmed orbiting a Sun-like star. As a planet orbits, its gravity causes its host star to wobble slightly. This wobble creates tiny but detectable shifts in the star’s spectrum. When the star moves towards Earth, its light is shifted slightly towards blue; when it moves away, the light shifts towards red. By measuring these changes, astronomers can tell if a planet is tugging on its star. Direct Imaging: Although extremely difficult, it is now possible to photograph some exoplanets. Using devices known as coronagraphs, telescopes can block out the intense light of the host star, allowing the very faint light of the planet to be captured. The forthcoming Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope , due to launch this August 30, will combine enormous wide-field surveys with microlensing observations and a sophisticated coronagraph technology. Together, these capabilities will help astronomers build a far broader statistical census of planetary systems while advancing our ability to image distant worlds directly. Artificial intelligence is also having an impact on modern astronomy; machine-learning algorithms can process the vast amounts of data collected by missions such as Kepler and TESS and help astronomers identify planetary signals hidden within enormous datasets. The Closest Exoplanets: Our Cosmic Neighbours Some of the most thrilling finds are the exoplanets closest to our solar system, offering us the best chance for detailed observation. Proxima Centauri b : This is the closest known exoplanet to Earth, orbiting the red dwarf star Proxima Centauri, a mere 4.2 light-years away in the Centaurus constellation. It is a rocky planet with a mass of at least 1.07 times that of Earth and orbits within its star’s habitable zone, the region where liquid water could potentially exist under the right conditions. However, its star emits powerful radiation, which could significantly challenge the planet’s potential habitability by eroding its atmosphere over time. Barnard b : This recently confirmed exoplanet orbits Barnard’s Star, the closest single red dwarf star to our Sun, located about six light-years away in the Ophiuchus constellation. It is a low-mass, rocky world, less than half the mass of Venus, that completes an orbit in 3.2 Earth days, indicating that it is extremely close to its star. With an estimated temperature of around 125°C, it is far too hot to support liquid surface water and lies well inside the habitable zone. Ross 128 b : This planet orbits an inactive, quiet red dwarf star 11 light-years away in the Virgo constellation. It is around 40% more massive than Earth and is one of the nearest temperate exoplanets, as well as the closest known to orbit an inactive red dwarf. Its estimated temperature could potentially allow liquid water under the right atmospheric conditions, although scientists remain uncertain whether it lies within its star’s habitable zone. The Most Earth-Like Contenders While the closest planets are not necessarily like Earth, astronomers have identified several more distant candidates that share key characteristics with our world, such as rocky compositions or locations within their stars’ habitable zones. LHS 1140 b : Located about 48 light-years away in the Cetus constellation, this “super-Earth” (a planet larger than Earth but smaller than Neptune) is considered one of the most promising potentially habitable exoplanets discovered. In July 2026, astronomers reported detecting helium escaping from the planet’s upper atmosphere, providing direct evidence that the planet has retained an atmosphere. Its red dwarf host star is also relatively quiet compared with many others of its type. TRAPPIST-1 System : This remarkable system, about 40 light-years away, is home to seven Earth-sized planets orbiting a single, cool red dwarf star in the Aquarius constellation. Three of these planets—TRAPPIST-1e, f and g—orbit within the traditional habitable zone. Their similarity in size and mass to Earth makes them prime targets in the search for life. Their proximity to their star also means they are probably tidally locked, with one side continually facing the star. Kepler-186f : The historic first validated Earth-sized planet found inside a habitable zone. It orbits its red dwarf star with a period of about 130 days, around 500 light-years away in the Cygnus constellation. Its great distance places it far beyond the handful of nearby rocky worlds whose atmospheres can currently be studied in detail. Kepler-452b : Often called “Earth’s cousin”, this exoplanet orbits a Sun-like star approximately 1,400 light-years away in the Cygnus constellation. It is about 60% larger than Earth and orbits at a similar distance from its star, with a period of 385 days. It was the first near-Earth-sized planet confirmed within the habitable zone of a star very similar to our Sun. Kepler-1649c : This Earth-sized exoplanet is located about 300 light-years away in the Cygnus constellation. It orbits its red dwarf star within the habitable zone, making it an intriguing candidate in the continuing search for potentially habitable worlds. LHS 1140 b now stands out as one of the leading candidates for the study of true habitability. It stands out because it is not merely “Earth-like”; it is one of the very few worlds where multiple independent observations point toward a stable atmosphere and a global ocean, both essential for long-term habitability. Proxima Centauri b is still an exciting possibility because it is so close, making it an obvious target for future interstellar missions. However, its severe radiation environment means it remains a high-risk candidate for habitability. Artist impression showing the exoplanet LHS 1140b, orbiting a red dwarf star around 48 light-years away. Credit: ESO/spaceengine.org What Makes a World Truly Habitable? Liquid water is one of the key requirements for life as we know it. A star’s “habitable zone” therefore describes the range of distances where liquid water could persist on a planet’s surface, provided that the planet also has a suitable atmosphere. But that is only the beginning of the question of whether a world could truly remain habitable over aeons. Since most of the nearest candidates revolve around red dwarf stars, and red dwarfs are smaller and dimmer than the Sun, their habitable zones lie very close to the star. This brings special challenges, such as tidal locking, in which a planet always shows the same face to its star—just as the Moon always shows the same side to Earth. Without sufficient atmospheric or oceanic circulation, this could create dramatic temperature differences between the permanent day side and night side. A substantial atmosphere, however, could redistribute heat and moderate those extremes. Another challenge is stellar flares: young red dwarfs can erupt in blasts of ultraviolet and X-ray radiation, similar to the solar storms we experience on Earth, but much stronger and more frequent. These eruptions can erode planetary atmospheres over time, making it more difficult for life as we know it to survive. When scientists assess whether a world might be genuinely habitable, they therefore consider much more than its position around its star. Liquid water, a steady source of energy, a stable atmosphere, useful chemical ingredients such as carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen, geological processes, magnetic protection and long-term environmental stability can all influence whether life could emerge, survive and evolve. For advanced, complex life, additional factors matter, such as low levels of catastrophic events (asteroid impacts, supernovae), moderate climate variability, and sufficient planetary mass to retain atmosphere and liquid water for billions of years. In the coming decades, astronomy will enter a new phase with the development of powerful, purpose-built observatories aimed at finding answers. NASA’s Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) , currently envisaged for the 2040s, is being designed specifically to search for Earth-like planets around nearby Sun-like stars and analyse their atmospheres for potential signs of life. For now, when we search the cosmos, we’re looking for Earth’s twin. But the most truly habitable world of all may be one we wouldn’t even recognise at first glance. There is also an increasing effort to create methods for detecting life that do not rely on the particular chemistry of Earth. Scientists are exploring so-called “ agnostic biosignatures ”, including forms of chemical complexity and organisation that living systems might produce even if alien biology uses very different building blocks from our own. Artist impression showing an exoplanet orbiting its star in the habitable zone. Credit: NASA A Universe of Possibilities The hunt for planets outside our solar system is a story of continuous discovery and ever-advancing technology; from the very first daring detections to AI-assisted analysis of enormous astronomical datasets, we are moving ever closer to answering that old question: are we alone? Exactly how many known worlds qualify as “potentially habitable” depends strongly on how the term is defined. One recent analysis from late 2025 identified about 70 exoplanets whose estimated equilibrium temperatures could support liquid water under suitable conditions, a number expected to grow as new missions expand the planetary census. The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, currently due to launch on August 30, 2026, will be an important part of that next stage. The planets mentioned here are among the most promising prospects on this cosmic voyage; each is a distinct world offering a different insight into what a planet might be and bringing us closer to discovering a true “Earth 2.0”. Scientists press on in the search for our cosmic twin, seeking to unravel our origins, push the boundaries of human ingenuity and ultimately answer one of humanity’s oldest questions: is there another sky out there with eyes gazing back at us? Omara Williams is a nuclear and software engineer whose multi-award-winning debut science-fiction novel, The Space Traveller’s Lover , shot to international bestseller status. Outside of her literary pursuits, she enjoys stargazing and chasing total solar eclipses. Competitions Hot Articles Most Popular

http://www.euronews.com/2026/09/01/fake-.text: Nearly 5% of goods entering the EU are fake, costing businesses an estimated €83 billion annually. At the port of Alicante, OLAF and Spanish Customs officers sift through shipping containers, hunting for counterfeit products hidden in plain sight among legitimate trade. Experts describe illicit trade as a sophisticated global business model, no longer limited to luxury items but now spanning car parts, electronics, pharmaceuticals and food. Counterfeit car components pose particular risks, as they bypass safety testing entirely. Officials stress that buying fakes helps finance serious crimes, including drug and human trafficking, urging shoppers to think twice before chasing a bargain.

Photograph: Ben Birchall/PA Bristol Edward Colston’s remains likely to stay at Bristol church that could become community space Exclusive: Slave trader is interred at All Saints, which may be given a change of use after being closed for years Steven Morris Mon 21 Sep 2026 10.43 EDT Last modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 12.08 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Bones of the enslaver Edward Colston are likely to remain interred in a church in Bristol if and when the currently unused building is given a new lease of life as a community resource, it has emerged. The dean of Bristol, the Very Rev Mandy Ford , said Colston’s remains would probably stay where they were in All Saints church on one of Bristol’s busiest streets. Colston, who died in 1721, made headlines around the world in 2020 when his statue in the city centre was toppled during a Black Lives Matter protest and thrown into the harbour . The diocese of Bristol has been consulting with Bristolians over what to do with All Saints on Corn Street, which has been closed since 1984. While no final decision has yet been made, it seems likely it will be used as a space to reflect on the port’s connections with the slave trade – and Colston’s remains will stay where they are. Ford said: “There is very, very clear guidance which assumes that you don’t disturb remains that have been given Christian burial, except in exceptional circumstances and so the presumption is that they will stay where they are.” The dean said that if there was to be a radical rebuilding of the space there could be an argument to inter the remains elsewhere. “Otherwise the assumption is that Christian burial is permanent and that’s where they stay.” View image in fullscreen All Saints church in Bristol, where the remains of Edward Colston are interred. Photograph: Diocese of Bristol Ford brings deep expertise to the job of helping decide what happens to Colston’s bones, as when she worked in Leicester she was closely involved in the reinterment of Richard III’s remains after they were found in a car park there . She acknowledged people had different understandings of the theological or spiritual significance of human remains. “But it’s a Christian place of burial and we are a Christian church trying to do the right thing. This is the burial place of a human being who was involved in a practice which we recognise to be utterly sinful and wrong.” The question of what to do about sites connected to Colston in Bristol is a thorny one. After the Colston statue was thrown into the harbour, windows celebrating him were removed from two Bristol churches as the diocese declared the fall of the statue was a “signal” for it to take action. In the same year, Bristol’s concert hall was renamed Bristol Beacon, having previously been called Colston Hall. It is likely to be many months before a final decision is made over the fate of All Saints. But the dean said: “I think people do see that it has potential as a place of learning and also a place of reconciliation. From the work that we’ve been doing in the cathedral and the relationships and the conversations that we have, I think there’s a strong sense that there’s huge potential in Bristol to have difficult conversations and to build a better future on the basis of truth-telling about the past.” She added that work carried out at a new All Saints had the potential to sit alongside projects on Bristol’s history being done by institutions including the University of Bristol and Bristol Old Vic . Ford said: “I think one can see it as part of a much bigger picture, which I think is really important if Bristol’s going to have a peaceful and flourishing future as a civic space and as a city.” The Rev Anjali Kanagaratnam , who is leading the All Saints consultation, has been taking groups into the church. She said there had been a huge range of views. “Each extreme was covered from: ‘I never want to come back into this building’ to ‘Why haven’t I been told that this building is here? I need to bring my children.’ Some people find it a hard space to be in. Some were annoyed by the fact that they didn’t know it was there.” Kanagaratnam said it had been vital to hear the voices of people in Bristol that had been affected by transatlantic slavery but the church had also made sure it heard what people from other communities, such as white working-class areas in south Bristol. Kanagaratnam said there was great potential for All Saints to be a place of “truth-telling”. She added: “I think people do see that it has potential as a place of learning and also a place of reconciliation.” Explore more on these topics Bristol Slavery Anglicanism Heritage Black British culture England news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Bristol church repair opens up possibility of Edward Colston exhumation Edward Colston statue placed in quiet corner of Bristol museum Bristol University decides not to rename buildings linked to slavery Lake District tour boat firm accused of ‘censoring’ Windermere links to slavery How the fall of Edward Colston’s statue revolutionised the way British history is told Justin Welby defends £100m fund to address C of E’s past links to slavery Those who tore down Colston’s statue helped lead us to the truth about slavery and the monarchy King Charles urged to ‘take some responsibility’ for royal slavery links Laura Trevelyan urges King Charles to apologise for historical links to slave trade Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckn8.text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, US envoys Jared Kushner (left) and Steve Witkoff (right) met Volodymyr Zelensky in Dublin on Thursday evening By Harry Sekulich Published 2 hours ago Ukraine's president has welcomed a pledge from US envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, to include delegates from the European Union in the next round of peace talks with Russia. European leaders have expressed deepening security concerns this week, and Volodymyr Zelensky said bringing them into the talks would ensure the EU has a "voice" in negotiations. Kushner and Witkoff met Zelensky in Dublin on Thursday evening as part of a busy day of shuttle diplomacy - they met Vladimir Putin in Moscow earlier, who said that Russia's position on the war - and its demand for territory - has not changed. The meetings follow talks in Abu Dhabi last week that failed to reach a breakthrough in ending the war. But Thursday did see Russia and Ukraine agree to another prisoner exchange - the largest swap yet since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022. Kushner said it would return "thousands of people to their families", but further details like how many prisoners would be exchanged or a timeline, were not given. US envoys meet Zelensky in Dublin after talks with Putin in Moscow Published 7 hours ago Europe's security 'fundamentally reshaped' by war in Ukraine Published 13 hours ago Zelensky has for several years been calling for European delegates to be included in the peace talks, and says it makes sense because of Kyiv's longer-term ambition to join the European Union. On Thursday, Kushner said that the US has been "working very, very closely over the past several months with Europeans and I think that that's been very important." He added that he had stressed to Putin how important it is to have European delegates "at the table". "He's willing to give it a try," Kushner added. Ukraine and Europe have long been concerned about the current US government's commitment to European security and its softening towards the Kremlin. Moscow has been dismissive of European involvement, although Europeans have long argued that they are central to any post-war dynamics on their continent. Earlier on Thursday, Vice President of the European Commission Kaja Kallas, the EU's top diplomat, told BBC's Newshour the presence of a European delegate showed the Kremlin "now realised that Europe is a big player". Kallas also expressed doubts that there was Russian momentum towards a peace deal. Taoiseach (Irish Prime Minister) MicheÃ¡l Martin told a host of Euro leaders gathered in the Irish capital on Thursday that he believed the security of the region has been "fundamentally reshaped" by Russia's war. "Many member states [of the EU] feel an existential threat because of what has happened in Ukraine and the potential, if Ukraine was to fall, for further aggression on the European continent," he told reporters. Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine remains under control of Russian forces, and cross-border incursions are increasingly common. Tensions between the US and Ukraine were on display on Thursday before Witkoff and Kushner's meeting with Zelensky. Earlier, the Ukrainian leader said that the military was facing more "systematic" restrictions to Starlink's military-grade satellite service, Starshield, meaning Kyiv was struggling to intercept Russian jet-powered drones. The technology owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX company has played a vital role in government and military connectivity in Ukraine, and increasingly assists in facilitating communication on Ukraine's front line.
